questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To be half a year in Italy.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The website of University of Bologna seemed at first site to be pretty organized. However, I still found it quiet hard to find the correct information about which courses were available in the spring and also general information on incoming exhange. As an exchange students I could have taken an Italian language course for free, but since I received no information about the course, I unfortunately missed the deadline for registration.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The university provided sufficient help if I needed it - you just need to email them :) It was pretty easy to contact the international mobility office at the University by mail. Also, the professors were very helpful and will answer you by mail if you have any questions about the curriculum of the courses, timetables etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Unfortunately it is pretty hard to find accommodation in Bologna. We (my two friends from back home and I) were pretty lucky to get a tip from a Danish student who went on exchange in Bologna a couple a years ago, and we got in contact with an Italian man who had several apartments around the city. So I would recommend to talk with former Bologna exchange students. There are aslo several facebook groups, where I know people have founded accommodation.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Its hard, but in the end everyone I got to know in Bologna found a place in the end :)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Usually you will get the courses you want, which is really nice. The thing is, that you are actually free to change courses until you have registered for the exam. So if you feel unsatisfied with a course, you can easily swap to another (If you do this, I would still recommend to do it in the beginning of the course, otherwise you will probably miss some important learning)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
On most of the courses you can find information on
unibo.it
. On the website, it's a bit hard to see if the courses are available in the spring or autumn. To find this information, you probably have to go to the website of the specific program. Also be aware that even though the topic of the course is in English on the website, it may still be in Italian.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Unfortunately, a lot of the courses I wanted were held on the same time. However, when I finally found the courses that fitted my study plan, I got all of the courses I wanted! :)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would recommend not to start too earlier to figure out which courses you want to take. Because as most thing in Italy, the sufficient information will first be uploaded very late.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses was a bit too easy for MA students. There are usually not a lot of readings, which is uncommon for a UCPH student like me. Instead, there are more classes during the week, which is very nice, because you then see your class mates very often (which is a very good way to find new friends!)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The students play a more active role during classes. There are a lot of discussions between teacher and students, and a lot of student presentations as well.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
WOMEN'S MOVEMENTS WORLDWIDE - I MOVIMENTI DELLE DONNE NEL MONDO (6 ECTS)
HISTORY OF GLOBALIZATION AND CRIME (8 ECTS)
POWER RELATIONS AND VICTIMIZATION PROCESSES (8 ECTS)
SOCIAL STRATIFICATION AND ECONOMIC INEQUALITY (8 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you are interested in criminology, Università di Bologna provides very interesting courses. I had two criminological courses. First was called "History of Globalization and Crime" where the teacher gave an introduction in sociological theories on the topic, and applied it on cases related to globalization. Second course was "Power Relations and Victimization Processes", which focused primarily on theories about victimization, including victims of criminal actions, but also victims of more broader societal issues and transitional processes. 

I will also recommend the course "Social Stratification and Economic Inequality" if you are interested in a more "core" sociological topic. Here the focus is mostly on quantitative studies on social inequality, and you also get the opportunity to work with quantitative analyses in R as a part of the exam, which I enjoyed a lot.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I unfortunately had some troubles with the flights both when arriving and leaving Bologna, because of a cancelled flight and strike, so I had to buy double flight tickets.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and alkohol are veeeery cheap, which is very nice, but it also makes you buy more :))

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not you any of the offers the university offered for incoming exchange students. Though, I know there are a lot of initiatives both via ESN (Erasmus Student Network, Bologna) and IC, Bologna.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Parties, dinners, trips to other Italian cities etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Tandem! A lot of Italian young people would love to do language exchange, where you improve your Italian and they improve their English. I also did a lot of bouldering at Up Urban Climbing, where there was a small community of really nice Italian guys. Otherwise I will just recommend to explore Bologna's amazing cuisine and vibrant atmosphere.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are a great train system from Naples and up. So from Bologna, you can very easily go to Milan (1 hour), Florence (40 min), Rome (2 hour) and Naples (3 hours) by train.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, Italian people are some of the most friendly I know.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to all of your classes! It's a very easy way to get friends, and we usually went out for a gelato or a spritz after class.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: You have to get use to people being late for meet ups :) And to eat a 9 in the evening!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness, the pace and - of course - the food!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Shorts 
A fan 
Wine glass

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would recommend you to try and learn italian! I kind of regret that I didn't put a bigger effort in learning the language.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To enjoy Bologna

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language barrier (but you will figure it out any way)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy and remember "when in rome" :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
